newsitem.title: UK: IEA's Priddle sees no immediate oil supply crisis.
newsitem.headline: IEA's Priddle sees no immediate oil supply crisis.

text.p: International Energy Agency (IEA) executive director Robert Priddle said he did not see a crisis in prospect from the threat of an oil supply crunch but he expressed concern at the low level of consumer stocks.
"There is no crisis in prospect," he told an energy conference on the theme, Oil security: is the tension over? organised by the Royal Institute of International Affairs.
"There is every prospect that the market will rebalance without the interference of governments," he added.
"There is reassurance in the fact that markets are more transparent and the opportunity to respond is very fast."

Priddle said that while he was concerned about the low level of consumer stocks, particularly in the United States, there was a "comfortable cushion" of 130 days of net import cover among members of the IEA.
He said he found a "disturbing trend" in stock levels held by the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), where forward cover had fallen to 70 days of net imports from 90 days in 1989.
"We clearly see a trend in lower stocks held by companies," which was seen in the recent "fragility" of the heating oil market, Priddle said.

This made the market vulnerable to any supply interruption, particularly if one took into account countries outside the OECD (Organisation of Economic and Cooperation Development), especially in Asia where the need to secure oil supply was vital and where there was no stock policy in place.
Asked what impact U.S. sanctions against Iran and Libya were likely to have on the security of future supplies, Priddle said this might have an impact on future capacity.
"Clearly if the U.S. policy works, then it is going to have an effect on the development of the additional capacity of these countries. It is a reasonable concern," he said.
Priddle added that he believed the U.S. policy was also likely to feed the scepticism of countries like China on the question of international energy cooperation.

He also said members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) were producing above their self-imposed ceiling and the market had the added security of 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) of spare capacity to fall back on even without Iraq, whose exports remain under a U.N. embargo.
This was enough to make up for any "significant supply loss," Priddle said.
"Several members of OPEC are producing well in excess of their ceiling," he said, adding that OPEC was no longer "an effective cartel."
In five years' time, non-OPEC producers would be able to meet the estimated five million bpd rise in global oil demand, Priddle said.
Recalling that the IEA had released oil from stocks during the 1990 Gulf crisis, Priddle said he did not believe concerted government action would be the answer to dealing with a supply interruption.

But Priddle said this did not mean an absence of risk, particularly from the Middle East where tension in Iraq continued, the United States had up to 12,000 troops in the region and Gulf producers were facing demographic problems from rising populations and lower oil revenue.
"I suggest that the political risk remains of a supply interruption and the question is how will the market cope with it," he said.

The only way to hedge against any supply interruptions having an impact on consumers was better information and coordination not only within the IEA but also with non-members, including OPEC producers.
Priddle also said he would like to see IEA membership expanded to countries outside the OECD and said South Korea was a prospective member.
"If we are going to intervene, we should do so globally. OECD membership is not enough," he added.
